query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at.% vanadium to equal-atomic NbMoTaW to form a NbMoTaWV quintenary alloy modifies local lattice distortions and dislocation core structures, thereby reducing the barriers for dislocation nucleation and motion at room temperature. This improved dislocation behavior enhances ductility without altering the high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance or irradiation resistance inherent to the parent alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW exhibiting a single-phase BCC structure with excellent high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.conditions: The NbMoTaWV alloy must maintain a uniform, equiatomic distribution with 5 at.% V substitution under controlled synthesis conditions to ensure a single-phase BCC structure. Tests should be conducted at room temperature, at 1600 °C, and under irradiation exposure conditions comparable to those used in previous studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Alteration of local lattice distortions and modification of dislocation core structures due to the presence of vanadium.
generation.mechanism: The addition of V is expected to change the dislocation-solute interaction energy in the alloy, lowering the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation and motion at room temperature. This results in improved ductility. The similar high configurational entropy and retention of the BCC structure help ensure that the high-temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance—both linked to the alloy’s defect formation energies and defect dynamics—are not compromised.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the NbMoTaWV alloy will exhibit a significant increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher strain-to-failure) while showing comparable yield strength and structural stability at 1600 °C and after irradiation exposure.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW with known excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance but poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds if the V content remains around 5 at.% and does not induce secondary phase formation or significant compositional segregation. Deviations from the single-phase BCC structure may invalidate the expected mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in ductility, as well as the subtle effects on dislocation dynamics and irradiation defect kinetics, require experimental validation. There is also some uncertainty if slight changes in electron density and shear modulus could subtly affect high-temperature strength or irradiation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of baseline equal-atomic NbMoTaW and one set of NbMoTaWV with approximately 5 at.% V addition, ensuring both are single-phase BCC. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to evaluate ductility (strain-to-failure), conduct mechanical tests at 1600 °C to measure yield and ultimate strengths, and expose samples to controlled irradiation (e.g., ion irradiation) followed by microstructural analysis of defect densities and lattice parameter shifts.
measurements: High-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths at 1600 °C
Irradiation-induced defect density and lattice parameter changes (via TEM or XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbMoTaWV alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility without a measurable degradation in high-temperature mechanical performance or increased irradiation damage relative to the NbMoTaW baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast to conventional alloys, SP-CSAs are composed of two to five-principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios that form random solid solutions in either a simple face-centred cubic (f.c.c.) or simple body-centred cubic (b.c.c.) crystal lattice structure. The complicated random arrangement of alloying elements and local chemical environment at atomic level lead SP-CSAs to exhibit extraordinary properties compared with traditional alloys, such as high thermal stability and hardness, high strength-to-weight ratio, high-temperature strength, great wear and fatigue resistance, and also excellent corrosion resistance. In addition, the high-level site-to-site lattice distortions and compositional complexities in SP-CSAs can effectively reduce the mean free path of electrons, phonons and magnons; these distortions and complexities can also be used to modify formation energies, migration barriers and diffusion pathways of irradiation-induced defects, thereby modifying defect generation, interaction, interstitial–vacancy recombination in the early stages of irradiation.
